b: Dan Spengler is a fisheries biologist and a 16-year project engineer for Berkley Tackle’s lure development. His longtime college pal and fishing buddy Dustin Toy is a federal wildlife biologist.

The two men were all-day fishing a South Dakota natural lake chain on Oct. 25 from Spengler’s Crestliner aluminum fishing boat. Using forward-facing sonar, they were on the lookout for some big walleyes.
But that morning had followed a freezing cold front with a bitter chill, spitting rain, and sometimes snow. The walleye bite was deep, slow, and tough.

“It was bitter cold, my hands were nearly frozen, the water temperature was 51 degrees and the fish were finicky — until I started using a lure I developed that proved deadly,” the 42-year-old Spirit Lake, Iowa, resident told Wired2fish. “I was marking fish on sonar, but they were locked to the bottom. They didn’t want to take the lures we usually used.”
The anglers caught a few walleyes with jigs and swim baits. But it was a grind until Spengler thought to use a lure he developed and tested last year. Berkley introduced the bait earlier this year.

“I thought of the Berkley Doom Stroller 70 because it’s a perfect lure for fish in post-cold-front conditions,” he explained. “So I tied on a Blue Shimmer color 70 and made a casting using a 7-foot spinning rod, 8-pound test braided line with 12-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

“I made a kind of pendulum retrieve as the lure falls, with my rod tip down. I designed this lure to be ‘strolled’ with the rod tip down, which allows a smooth rolling action. The lure has a feathered treble hook that gives it subtle action on the fall.”

Spengler said that he could catch almost every walleye he marked on sonar with just a cast or two of his Doom Stroller 70, which weighs 2/5-ounce but casts well like a jig on spinning tackle and sinks about two feet per second.

The Doom Stroller started out as bait for another species. But Spengler — who’s also an accomplished panfish angler — knew that the “very versatile lure with lots of seasonal fishing applications” was great for walleye, too.

“I really developed this lure for bass fishing with pro Logan Park,” he began. “It’s an alternative to a jig and minnow for walleyes, and the flash-and-roll it has makes it a deadly finesse bait. I tested a prototype Doom Stroller last year and made five casts and caught three big walleyes.”

“The way it flashes and rolls is very natural, looking just like a minnow,” Spengler continued. “Once I saw a sonar fish on bottom, I’d cast to it — and when the fish would engage the lure, I’d bring my rod tip up. This makes the lure suspend even in deep water.”
That triggered a strike even on those deep post-cold-front walleyes, and they caught about a dozen. Most were six to eight pounds, and the two anglers released them all.
